newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia seen to become booming Balkan car market.
newsitem.headline: Croatia seen to become booming Balkan car market.

text.p: Croatia is emerging from the ruins of the wars in former Yugoslavia as the fastest-growing car market in the Balkans, according to automakers attending a car show that opens in Zagreb on Monday.

"In previous years, it was a tough market because of the fighting -- I had to stop travelling here for a while because it had become too dangerous," said Patrick Fourdrain, sales manager for ex-Yugoslavia at U.S. carmaker Ford Motor Co.

"But foreign investors and tourists are returning to pour money into the economy, especially near the Adriatic coastline, and I expect parts of the country to really boom. Croatia should outperform the rest of the region in market growth."
Zagreb has staged car shows annually since 1992 despite periodic fighting with rebel Serbs. The current show runs through April 13.

As a member of the socialist federation of Yugoslavia until 1991, Croatia shunned the global auto industry under a protected economy that in the 1980s levied onerous import duties on new cars -- often topping 100 percent.

However, since the Dayton accord to end the war in Bosnia was signed in 1995, Croatia has become a magnet for automakers desperate to find new outlets for their excess manufacturing capacity in western Europe.
Import duties on new cars now stand between 10 and 15 percent -- one of the lowest tariff regimes anywhere in the old East bloc. And trade liberalisation has sparked a battle.
German automotive group Volkswagen AG and Italian conglomerate Fiat SPA -- number one and number two respectively in new car sales in western Europe -- are dueling for market leadership in Croatia.
In 1996, VW outsold Fiat 3,704 units to 3,032 units.
But all automakers are looking for part of the action, as most expect the market to soar above 50,000 units at the turn of the century from 21,179 units last year.
"This market will easily double within five years," said Tom Olmsted, an operations director for southeast Europe at German automaker Adam Opel AG, a subsidiary of U.S. automaker General Motors Corp.
"The economic situation is improving, industrial output is up, interest rates are stable and unemployment is falling," he added. "This is a good environment for growth."

Opel forecast significant improvements in Croatia's main economic indicators between 1996 and 2000, including a rise in per-capita gross domestic product (GDP) to $6,000 from $4,400 and a fall in the jobless rate to 10 percent or less from 16 percent, Olmsted said.

Since the end of communism, new vehicle sales have exploded throughout central and eastern Europe, where throngs of consumers are still saving money to buy their first modern automobile. Per-capita car ownership in the region remains under half the levels in western Europe.

Croatia borders a sub-region of the most vibrant markets, the Central European Free Trade Agreement (CEFTA), where sales grew nearly 40 percent in 1996 to 842,565 units. CEFTA includes the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, Slovakia and Slovenia.
Croatia, home to 4.7 million people, is alone among Balkan countries expected to enjoy similar growth, even though some of these markets dwarf Croatia in population.
Romania, which has 22 million people, likely will increase new vehicle sales only 13 percent to 90,000 units in 2000 from 80,000 units in 1996, Olmsted said.

And Bulgaria, whose population is 8.4 million, might not reach in 2000 the current volume of vehicles sold in Croatia. In 1996, Bulgaria's market barely edged above 8,600 units, according to British automotive consultants Harbour Wade Brown.
Other markets already might have seen their best days.

Slovenia, the region's wealthiest country with half the population of Croatia, sold over 65,000 new vehicles in 1996 and 1995 -- triple Croatia's market. But Slovenia's current sales levels, a huge leap over the 47,000 units sold in 1994, are expected to stay fairly flat the next five years.
Despite its potential, Croatia remains one of the few countries in central and eastern Europe not to produce cars, including Albania and Macedonia.

But some automakers believe car production in Croatia is feasible, and VW's executive-car unit Audi AG recently has been rumored to be considering this possiblity. Audi has already shown interest in assembling its A3 cars in Macedonia.
